newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Irish present new compromise over veal crate ban.
newsitem.headline: Irish present new compromise over veal crate ban.

text.p: Ireland presented a new compromise on Tuesday over proposals to phase out veal crates and improve the diet of calves, diplomats said.
They said the presidency was making a major effort to forge an agreement that would satisfy France, the main user of veal crates.
France is linking agreement to changes in weight limits for early marketing subsidies for calves after French farmers went on the rampage on Monday.
France also wants proposed diet changes to be modified to ensure the continued production of white meat prized by consumers.
Other problems, which also concern Italy, are the size of the crates and the time period for phasing them out.
The Commission proposed in January 1996 banning new and renovated crates from 1998 and all crates by 2008.

French farmers complain that new early marketing subsidies, which encourage the slaughter of calves younger than usual to cut the amount of beef on an EU market depressed by the mad cow crisis, favour Dutch breeders.
The subsidies go to producers who cut 15 percent off the average normal weight of calves at slaughter -- but the average varies from country to country.

Dutch breeders, whose calves usually weigh more than 160 kg (350 lbs), get a subsidy for producing a calf of 138 kg (300 lbs) or less, for instance, while the French producers only qualify with calves weighing 108 kg (240 lbs) or less.
French officials said that Denmark, Sweden and Italy also had problems with the early marketing premium.

Member state experts were studying the new Irish compromise while ministers discussed a Commission proposal to ban material, such as brain, spinal cord and spleen, from sheep likely to be infected with scrapie.
Scrapie is a brain wasting disease similar to mad cow disease -- Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE). Recent British and French research has shown that sheep could catch BSE.
